articles.title: Whale swimming evolution recorded in vertebral microanatomy from the Eocene to present.
articles.authors: Lene Liebe Delsett, Justin J L Kimball, Vanja Simonsen et al.
articles.abstract: Among modern aquatic amniote clades that evolved pelagic locomotion, whales are a prime example, but timing and mode of evolutionary changes in their swimming are poorly understood. Here, we use 3D vertebral microanatomy derived from CT scanning to investigate swimming patterns in extinct whales. All vertebral centra from a single specimen of the extant common dolphin Delphinus delphis were used to provide a baseline for the correlation of microanatomical parameters and spinal movements in our dataset of fossil whales. We find that bone anisotropy, and to some extent bone compactness, mirrors the amount of compression and movement in vertebral regions. We use these parameters to infer regional movements and thus swimming mode for several lineages of stem cetaceans (Natchitochia jonesi, Pachycetus wardi, Zygorhiza kochii) and crown cetaceans (Maiabalaena nesbittae, an undescribed Oligocene odontocete and a modern minke whale). Natchitochia jonesi could walk on land, whereas Pachycetus wardi and Zygorhiza kochii were obligately aquatic, but show more spinal flexibility than modern taxa. The early Oligocene mysticete and odontocete differ in microstructural properties and might have experienced a different trajectory towards their extant bauplans. Overall, microanatomical data confirm increasing pelagic specializations in cetacean evolution that include a stiffer torso, but our data also highlight modular patterns of compactness within vertebral regions. Our approach is promising for future use of three-dimensional vertebral microanatomical data to understand locomotory patterns.

articles.title: An investigation of the functional significance of the pyramidalis muscle using shear wave elastography.
articles.authors: Craig L Short, Troy Morrison, Tania N Crotti et al.
articles.abstract: The pyramidalis (Py) is a small triangular-shaped anterior abdominal wall muscle, the function of which remains uncertain. We used brightness-mode (B-mode) ultrasound to determine Py prevalence and tested the hypothesis that Py contributed to stiffness of the linea alba (LA) using shear wave elastography (SWE). Py prevalence was observed and documented using conventional B-mode ultrasound in 20 participants (7 male). LA stiffness was measured using SWE with Py relaxed and during Py contraction in 10 of the participants (3 male, mean [SD] age 26.3 ± 8.0 years). Py activity was controlled using neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES), while lower rectus abdominis activity was monitored using electromyography (EMG). Py was present bilaterally in 15 of 20 (75%) participants, unilaterally in 2 (10%) and absent in 3 (15%). A statistically significant difference (p < 0.002) in the mean LA stiffness was observed when comparing SWE measurements of the Py at relaxed (15.7 kPa ± 6.1 kPa, 95% CI 11.4-20.1 kPa) and during contraction (24.2 kPa ± 10.8 kPa, 95% CI 16.5-32.0 kPa). No statistically significant difference in lower rectus abdominis activity was observed between the presence and absence of NMES (p = 0.517), indicating accurate and isolated Py stimulation. Our results indicate that Py muscle is commonly present (75% participants) and that Py contraction results in a significant increase in LA stiffness, supporting the previously unvalidated hypothesis that the function of Py, at least in part, is to increase LA stiffness and contribute to the biomechanics of the trunk.

articles.title: Anatomical and histological characterization of the heart of the scarlet ibis (Eudocimus ruber).
articles.authors: Beatriz Rosa Silva, Maria Gabriela Aparecida Farias Pereira, Max Alex Santos Ferreira et al.
articles.abstract: Detailed information on the cardiac morphology of the scarlet ibis (Eudocimus ruber) remains limited. This study aimed to characterize the gross and microscopic anatomy of this species' heart and provide morphometric data. We examined six specimens (three males and three females) using gross anatomical analysis, morphometry, conventional radiography, three-dimensional scanning, light microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. The mean heart mass was 5.93 ± 1.49 g (n = 6), corresponding to 1.10 ± 0.23% of body mass, and the mean radiographic cardiothoracic ratio was 66.90 ± 5.78% (n = 3). Macroscopic examination identified three venae cavae: the right and left cranial venae cavae and the caudal vena cava. The left atrioventricular valve had two cusps with chordae tendineae and papillary muscles, whereas the right atrioventricular valve had a single muscular fold. Histological examination identified uninucleated and binucleated Purkinje fibers in the subendocardial region, extending into myocardial muscle bundles. The base of the aorta showed hyaline cartilage containing chondrocytes and chondroblasts, with no bone tissue identified in the examined sections. These findings provide anatomical, morphometric, and histological data on the heart of E. ruber and a basis for future comparative studies of avian cardiac morphology.

articles.title: Cross bridges, tendons and titin: evolving roles in muscle mechanics.
articles.abstract: All fields of science evolve over time as interpretation of the evidence changes with the discovery of new facts, and muscle physiology is no exception. Ideas once thought preposterous may eventually become accepted dogma, as was the case for the sliding filament theory itself. The currently accepted sliding-filament - swinging cross-bridge paradigm views muscles as motors with static isometric force-length and isotonic force-velocity properties that necessarily limit their ability to store and recover viscoelastic energy. These limitations understandably led to the plausible explanation that tendons must be responsible for energy storage and recovery. However, recent advances in technology have enabled investigation of muscle properties in moving humans and other animals, providing significant new data on dynamic muscle function. Bridging the gap between laboratory studies of ex vivo muscle preparations and in vivo muscle mechanics has resulted in a paradigm shift toward the idea that muscles are tunable viscoelastic actuators that can harvest substantial energy from interactions with the environment. Here, we provide a somewhat chronological account of the contentious history of the field of muscle physiology and the evolution of ideas about muscle function, focusing particularly on muscle viscoelastic properties and energy storage. We argue that accumulating data position titin as a length- and activation-dependent viscoelastic element whose properties can be inferred from, and indeed are critical for, in vivo muscle function. We also provide ideas for future directions to stimulate progress in understanding titin's role in dynamic muscle function.

articles.title: Biomechanical link between knee osteoarthritis and lumbar spine loading: An experimental and simulation-based analysis.
articles.authors: Ali Jamshidian, Alireza Rouyin, Hamed Nazemi et al.
articles.abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and low back pain (LBP) frequently co-occur, yet their biomechanical link remains unclear. This exploratory study investigated whether KOA gait is associated with altered trunk muscle forces and lumbar loading. Motion-capture and ground-reaction-force data were collected from eight individuals with mild-to-moderate medial KOA and ten healthy controls. Participant-scaled OpenSim models were used to estimate trunk muscle forces and lumbar joint reaction forces (JRFs). Between-group comparisons used Mann-Whitney U tests with false-discovery-rate correction. Walking speed did not differ between groups, whereas stride length was shorter in KOA (q = 0.033). Proximal kinematic differences were limited: no pelvic variable remained significant after correction, and only mean thoracic lateral bending differed (q = 0.032), with a small absolute magnitude. Mean knee angle differed between groups (q = 0.014), with additional differences in peak knee and ankle kinematics (q ≤ 0.006). Model-predicted mean and peak multifidus, longissimus, and iliocostalis forces were greater in KOA, whereas internal oblique forces were lower (all q < 0.05). Mean and peak lumbar compression were greater in KOA at all six levels from T12-L1 to L5-S1 (all raw p < 0.001; q < 0.05), and anterior-posterior JRFs were greater at selected levels. These higher muscle forces and JRFs, despite limited group-level proximal kinematic differences, may reflect attenuation or cancellation of heterogeneous individual gait adaptations during averaging, even though these adaptations may still influence internal mechanical demands.

articles.title: Feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability in people with chronic ankle instability during single-leg landing.
articles.authors: Tsz Yin Li, Zhuoran Wang, Reece Cascoe et al.
articles.abstract: Individuals with chronic ankle instability(CAI) show deficits in neuromuscular control and postural stability. While feedback mechanisms are well-studied, feedforward mechanisms during dynamic tasks remains underexplored. This study compared feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability among CAI, coper and healthy groups. Fifteen CAI(23.5 ± 2.9 years, 11 M/4F), fifteen coper(24.1 ± 3.4 years, 12 M/3F) and fifteen healthy participants(25.5 ± 3.5 years, 11 M/4F) performed single-leg drop landings from 30 cm. Total centre of pressure movement during 1-second and 3-second(TOTEX1s&TOTEX3s), mediolateral sway distance(DML), peak vertical GRF(peak vGRF) and root-mean-square of mediolateral GRF in the first 0.4 s(RMS_ML_0.4) were recorded via force plate. Surface electromyography recorded muscle activity 200 ms before landing among tibialis anterior(TA), peroneus longus(PL) and gastrocnemius lateralis(GL). Pre-activation timing was calculated using the Teager-Kaiser energy operator(TKEO). Statistical analysis involved one-way ANOVA(α = 0.05) and Tukey post-hoc testing. Compared to healthy participants, CAI individuals displayed earlier TA(270 ± 73 ms vs. 85 ± 53 ms, p < 0.001) and PL(260 ± 87 ms vs. 102 ± 62 ms, p < 0.001) pre-activations, alongside higher TA activity(76 ± 27% vs. 35 ± 19%, p < 0.001) but lower PL activity(38 ± 14% vs. 77 ± 23%, p < 0.001). Higher RMS_ML_0.4(6.7 ± 1.3%BW vs. 5.6 ± 1.0%BW, p = 0.037), DML(55.6 ± 15.7 mm vs. 39.5 ± 9.0 mm, p < 0.001) and peak vGRF(334 ± 44%BW vs. 286 ± 59%BW, p = 0.041)were observed as well. Coper showed earlier GL pre-activation(169 ± 57 ms vs. 108 ± 67 ms, p = 0.021), increased activity(155 ± 40% vs. 97 ± 29%, p < 0.001) and decreased DML(42.7 ± 7.0 mm vs. 55.6 ± 15.7 mm, p = 0.008) compared to CAI individuals. CAI exhibited postural control deficits and ineffective feedforward control, shown by lower PL activity despite early pre-activation. Rate of force production training is advised. Increased GL activation may serve as a compensatory response in copers after initial ankle sprain.

articles.title: Associations between countermovement jump impulse and running kinetics following ACL reconstruction.
articles.authors: Sami Ghani, Eve-Merina Lucron, Long Yiu Chan et al.
articles.abstract: Persistent deficits in lower-limb loading are commonly observed following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and may influence running biomechanics. Countermovement jump (CMJ) impulse can provide a phase-specific measure of force-time characteristics to reflect limb loading capacity; however, its relationship with running kinetics remains unclear. This study aimed to quantify phase-specific CMJ impulse following ACLR and examine associations with vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) metrics during treadmill running at the return-to-running phase. Forty-two participants performed three unilateral and bilateral CMJs on dual force plates and ran at 8 km/hr on an instrumented treadmill. Concentric, eccentric braking, and landing impulses were calculated. Running variables included weight acceptance rate, weight acceptance peak force, and maximum applied force. Inter-limb differences were assessed using Wilcoxon/paired t-tests. Impulse-vGRF relationships were analysed using Pearson/Spearman correlations and multiple linear regression. The ACLR limb exhibited significant deficits across all unilateral and bilateral CMJ phases, except for unilateral landing impulse. Deficits were greatest for unilateral concentric impulse (Δ1.3Ns·kg-0.67, d = 1.49, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force limb symmetry index (LSI) was explained by unilateral concentric impulse LSI (adjusted R2 = 0.25, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric impulse (adjusted R2 = 0.38, p < 0.001). Weight acceptance peak force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric and landing impulses (adjusted R2 = 0.37, p < 0.001). No meaningful relationships were observed for eccentric impulses or weight acceptance rate metrics. These findings indicate that jump impulse testing may provide clinically relevant indicators of running kinetics.

articles.title: MyotonPRO-derived hamstring mechanical properties across testing positions and their associations with maximal strength.
articles.authors: Shani Herszfang, Noam Avitan, Alon Kalron
articles.abstract: The MyotonPRO is increasingly used to quantify skeletal muscle mechanical properties; however, hamstring measurements may vary across testing positions, and the relationships between these measurements and maximal strength remain unclear. This study investigated differences in MyotonPRO-derived mechanical properties of the biceps femoris and semitendinosus across four testing positions and examined their exploratory associations with maximal isometric hamstring strength. Thirty healthy adults (18 males, 12 females; age 27.4 ± 4.9 years) underwent MyotonPRO assessment in the prone position, prone with the knee flexed to 90°, bilateral standing, and single-leg standing. Oscillation frequency, dynamic stiffness, logarithmic decrement, relaxation time, and creep were measured in both muscles. Maximal isometric hamstring strength was assessed using the End Range Hamstring Strength Test with handheld dynamometry. MyotonPRO-derived mechanical properties differed significantly across testing positions, with large position effects (partial η2 = 0.355-0.822). Stiffness and oscillation frequency generally increased toward weight-bearing positions, whereas relaxation time and creep decreased; logarithmic decrement showed a less consistent pattern. Exploratory correlation analyses showed moderate-to-strong associations between maximal hamstring strength and stiffness, frequency, and relaxation time, as well as creep (|r| = 0.38-0.67), whereas logarithmic decrement showed weaker and more variable associations. In an exploratory hierarchical regression, adding logarithmic decrement to the selected stiffness measure increased R2 from 0.440 to 0.500, but the incremental change was not statistically significant (ΔR2 = 0.060, p = 0.082). These findings indicate that MyotonPRO-derived hamstring mechanical properties differ across testing positions and should therefore be interpreted within standardized testing conditions.

articles.title: Physiological Adaptations to Controlled Work Rate Heat Acclimation Do Not Differ Between Highly Trained Male and Female Endurance Runners.
articles.authors: Marcos S Keefe, Ryan A Dunn, Danielle E Levitt et al.
articles.abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine whether the trajectory and magnitude of physiological adaptation to controlled work rate heat acclimation (HEAT) differ between male and female highly trained endurance runners, while comparing adaptations with work rate matched temperate exercise training (TEMP). Eighteen highly trained endurance runners (8 males, 10 females) completed two seven-session interventions consisting of HEAT (40°C, 35% relative humidity [RH]) and TEMP (22°C, 35% RH) in a randomized, counterbalanced crossover design. Each session consisted of 60 min of running at 50% of velocity at maximal oxygen uptake. Physiological adaptation was quantified as the change (Δ) relative to session 1 for core temperature (Tc), skin temperature, heart rate (HR), whole-body sweat rate (WBSR), and plasma volume (PV). No intervention × sex × session interactions were observed for Tc, HR, or WBSR (p > 0.05), indicating that the trajectory of adaptation did not differ between sexes or interventions. Likewise, no sex differences in the overall magnitude of adaptation were observed for any HEAT outcome. Significant main effects of intervention demonstrated greater reductions in mean and peak Tc; baseline, mean, and peak HR; as well as greater increases in WBSR during HEAT compared with TEMP (p < 0.05). PV did not change following either intervention. Male and female highly trained endurance runners exhibited comparable thermoregulatory and cardiovascular adaptation to controlled work rate heat acclimation. Although work rate matched temperate exercise induced partial physiological adaptation, environmental heat stress enhanced the overall adaptation magnitude without altering the adaptation trajectory between sexes.

articles.title: Neonatal stress is associated with region-specific changes in mitochondrial respiration and sex-dependent respiratory instability in adulthood.
articles.authors: Antonia Vallejo Puerta, Lida Sanchez, Fernanda Aliaga-Raduan et al.
articles.abstract: Early-life stress is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of brain development, yet its long-term impact on the neural control of breathing remains poorly defined. Here we show that neonatal maternal separation (NMS, P3-P12) induces long-term alterations in respiratory stability and mitochondrial function within respiratory circuits. In adulthood, NMS altered respiratory stability, with significant treatment × sex interactions for total and postsigh apnoeas; post hoc comparisons showed increased frequencies of these apnoeic events in males. Sigh frequency also showed a significant main effect of treatment. Region-specific high-resolution respirometry showed that NMS was associated with reduced mitochondrial respiration in the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH) and increased mitochondrial respiration in the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) and ventral respiratory column (VRC), without significant treatment × sex interactions. Normalization to cytochrome c oxidase (COX) activity largely eliminated these differences, suggesting that changes in absolute respiration are consistent with a contribution of differences in mitochondrial content rather than major alterations in respiratory capacity relative to mitochondrial abundance. In the pre-Bötzinger complex, absolute mitochondrial respiration was preserved, whereas oxygen consumption rate (OCR)/COX ratios revealed treatment-dependent alterations in mitochondrial respiratory flux relative to mitochondrial content. NMS also altered the expression of selected genes involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy, fusion and fission in the NTS and VRC, with significant main effects of treatment and sex but no treatment × sex interactions. Oxidative and inflammatory markers were largely preserved, although selective effects of sex and treatment were detected. Together, these findings demonstrate that neonatal stress produces persistent, region-specific remodelling of mitochondrial and molecular pathways within respiratory circuits, accompanied by sex-dependent vulnerability to respiratory instability. KEY POINTS: Early-life stress induces a persistent, sex-dependent disruption of respiratory control, increasing apnoeas in adult males, whereas females remain comparatively resistant. This phenotype is associated with region-specific remodelling of mitochondrial function along the paraventricular hypothalamus (PVH)-brainstem axis, characterized by reduced hypothalamic respiration and increased brainstem mitochondrial respiration after neonatal stress. Neonatal stress alters transcriptional pathways involved in mitochondrial biogenesis, mitophagy and dynamics within respiratory brainstem regions, revealing persistent molecular remodelling associated with early-life adversity.

articles.title: Tissue-Specific Regulation of Glucose and Lipid Metabolism by miR-29a in Insulin Resistance and Type 2 Diabetes.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Mariazel Rubio-Valles, Brendan Egan, Everardo Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al.
articles.abstract: MicroRNA-29a (miR-29a) has emerged as a context-dependent regulator of glucose and lipid metabolism in insulin-sensitive tissues, yet its tissue-specific actions in insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes remain incompletely understood. We synthesized peer-reviewed evidence retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost on the role of miR-29a across skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, liver, and pancreatic β-cells. We first define the nomenclature and genomic organization of the miR-29 family, its upstream transcriptional regulators, and the Argonaute-based evidence that separates direct target repression from correlative association. Across these tissues, miR-29a modulates oxidative metabolism, inflammatory signaling, and mitochondrial adaptation, largely through the PPARδ/PGC-1α axis, exerting complex and sometimes opposing effects depending on the tissue environment. We further examine miR-29a as a mediator of interorgan communication through extracellular vesicles, its responsiveness to exercise, and its emerging value as a biomarker and therapeutic target, while highlighting unresolved contradictions and translational hurdles. Because miR-29 family members act as tumor suppressors in most epithelial tissues, we also address the oncogenic risk inherent in nucleic acid strategies that lower miR-29a levels. Collectively, this mini-review positions miR-29a as a physiology-oriented integrator of metabolic remodeling and tissue-specific adaptation in metabolic disease.

articles.title: Restitution properties during ventricular fibrillation and the effects of cardiac pacing location on ventricular electrophysiology in the rabbit heart.
articles.authors: Bethan Roper-Jones, Emily Allen, Rachel L Sutcliffe et al.
articles.abstract: Sudden cardiac death is a cause of mortality due to malignant arrhythmias such as ventricular fibrillation (VF). Although action potential duration (APD) restitution is a method to assess arrhythmic susceptibility, repolarisation may depend on prior activation history, a phenomenon known as cardiac memory. Cardiac memory describes the persistence of repolarisation effects from previous beats, such that APD reflects not only the immediately preceding diastolic interval (DI) but also earlier activation effects. This may be relevant during VF, where continuously varying activation patterns prevent a steady electrophysiological state. This study investigated how pacing location affects ventricular electrophysiology and whether repolarisation during VF exhibits short-term cardiac memory. Langendorff-perfused rabbit hearts were used to record monophasic action potentials from the left ventricular apex and base. Pacing was conducted from five sites. Steady-state APD was assessed during constant pacing. Effective refractory period (ERP), APD restitution and conduction time restitution (CTR) were assessed using an S1-S2 extra-stimulus protocol (S1, conditioning stimuli; S2, premature extra-stimulus). Additionally, APD-DI and APD-APD relationships were analysed during early VF. Pacing location significantly influenced S1 and S2 conduction delays, consistent with site-dependent activation timing. However, steady-state APD, ERP and CTR were not significantly affected by pacing location. In contrast, during VF, APD exhibited a significant dependence on preceding DI and preceding APD over approximately the first 30 beats, with these relationships progressively deteriorating thereafter. These findings demonstrate that while pacing location alters activation timing, repolarisation dynamics under stable activation histories are robust. During VF, continuously changing activation patterns unmask short-term cardiac memory.

articles.title: Exercise and physiological monitoring in isolated, confined and extreme environments and space analogues: A scoping review.
articles.authors: Gustavo S O Lima, Kaline V F Dinis, Leonardo P Silva et al.
articles.abstract: This scoping review synthesized evidence on physical activity/exercise and physiological monitoring in isolated, confined and extreme (ICE) environments, with emphasis on Antarctic missions and space analogues. ICE exposures combine cold stress, confinement, disrupted light-dark cycles and psychosocial strain, which can challenge musculoskeletal integrity, cardiovascular regulation, sleep/circadian function and cognition. Following Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidance, we searched Web of Science, Embase, Scopus and PubMed/Medline, complemented by grey literature and AI-assisted citation chasing. Eligible reports included human studies in ICE/analogue settings that implemented or quantified physical activity/exercise and/or physiological monitoring. Seventeen studies published between 2003 and 2025 met inclusion criteria and were mapped across ICE characteristics, exercise protocols, monitoring technologies, outcomes and research gaps. Exercise was reported as a potential countermeasure to attenuate selected aspects of deconditioning and support sleep and psychophysiological adaptation, particularly in bed rest and simulated confinement studies. Antarctic field studies more often characterized spontaneous physical activity, sleep/activity rhythms and field-adapted monitoring. Assessment strategies varied, ranging from self-reported logs and actigraphy in operational field settings to laboratory-grade measures in bed rest and simulated confinement studies. Overall, exercise emerged as a pragmatic, domain-specific countermeasure against deconditioning in ICE settings, with effectiveness varying by modality and physiological target. However, heterogeneity in exposure characterization, exercise dose and monitoring methods, despite feasible wearable-based capture of behavioural and physiological signals, limited comparability and mechanistic inference. Future ICE research should prioritize harmonized reporting, standardized monitoring and longitudinal designs linking exercise exposure to physiological, behavioural and operational outcomes.

articles.title: The Respiratory Compensation Point Predicts 19.2-km Cycling Performance in Trained Male Cyclists.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Yuet L I So, Robin Faricier, Nasimi A Guluzade et al.
articles.abstract: So, YLI, Faricier, R, Guluzade, NA, Belfry, GR, Murias, JM, and Keir, DA. The respiratory compensation point predicts 19.2-km cycling performance in trained male cyclists. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study tested the hypothesis that the step-ramp-step (SRS)-corrected cycling power output (PO) at the respiratory compensation point (RCP) predicts cycling time-trial performance and explored the independent and collective contributions to trial time of 4 physiological variables derived from single or repeated SRS protocols: peak oxygen uptake (V̇o2peak), cycling economy, RCP, and fatigue resistance. Twenty-eight trained male cyclists completed an SRS protocol before and after a 19.2-km virtual time trial (∼30 minutes) on their personal road bikes using a smart trainer. V̇o2peak, cycling economy, and SRS-corrected PO at RCP were derived from the pre-time-trial SRS protocol. Fatigue resistance was quantified as the change in peak ramp PO from pre- to post-time trial. Independent and multilinear regression evaluated the predictive strength of each variable. Relative SRS-corrected RCP (W·kg-1) showed the strongest independent correlation with time-trial completion time (r = -0.61, p < 0.001). Relative V̇o2peak (mL·kg-1·min-1) and cycling economy (%) were also moderately associated with time-trial performance (r = -0.42, p = 0.03; and r = -0.55, p < 0.001, respectively), whereas fatigue resistance was not significantly correlated. In the multilinear regression analysis, SRS-corrected RCP uniquely explained 30.9% of the model's total predictive variance (r = 0.68, p < 0.01) followed by cycling economy (21.3%), ΔPOpeak (2.1%), and absolute V̇o2peak (3.3%). Among trained male cyclists, relative PO at SRS-corrected RCP is a strong and independent predictor of ∼30-minute time-trial performance. The SRS protocol provides a practical, single-session method to assess key physiological determinants of endurance performance, with valuable applications for training prescription and athlete monitoring.

articles.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Brian Benitez, Minyoung Kwak, Pasquale J Succi et al.
articles.abstract: Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.
